title: Why Nicodemus Defended Jesus Before Following Him Publicly
paragraphs: Why Nicodemus Defended Jesus Before Following Him Publicly
Jerusalem was loud that week.
Not loud with worship.
Loud with suspicion.

Men whispered in corners. Religious leaders tightened their grip on influence. Crowds argued about miracles. Some called Jesus a prophet. Some called Him dangerous. Some wanted Him crowned. Others wanted Him buried.
And somewhere in the middle of all that pressure stood a man who could lose everything.
His name was Nicodemus.
Not a fisherman. Not a rebel. Not an outcast.
A Pharisee. A ruler. A respected teacher of Israel. A man with status to protect.
John 3:1 introduces him carefully:
“Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.”
The Greek text says:
Ἦν δὲ ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων Νικόδημος ὄνομα αὐτῷ, ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
The word ἄρχων (archōn) means ruler, authority figure, one carrying influence and governance.
Nicodemus was not casually religious. He was deeply embedded inside the spiritual power structure of Israel.
And yet… something about Jesus disturbed him in a way religion never could.
Not because Jesus lacked truth.
Because Jesus carried too much of it.
Most people remember Nicodemus for visiting Jesus at night. But very few stop to ask why.
Why would a respected Pharisee secretly seek out a controversial teacher? Why defend Jesus before openly following Him? Why risk association before making public commitment?
Because Nicodemus represents something painfully human.
The war between conviction and fear.
And if we are honest… many believers still live there.
Some people think faith begins publicly. Scripture often shows the opposite.
Sometimes faith begins in hidden trembling. Sometimes discipleship starts with dangerous curiosity. Sometimes people defend truth long before they have courage to stand completely inside it.
Nicodemus was watching Jesus long before he was ready to lose everything for Him.
And maybe that is exactly why this story still feels uncomfortably personal.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to believe quietly.
Quietly at work. Quietly around unbelieving family. Quietly around mocking friends. Quietly inside churches where appearance matters more than surrender.
You know Jesus is real. But you are terrified of what full obedience could cost.
Nicodemus understood that fear.
When he first approached Jesus, he came at night. The Greek phrase from John 3:2 says:
οὗτος ἦλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτὸς
Literally:
“He came to Him by night.”
Some scholars argue the timing was practical. Others see symbolism. John’s Gospel repeatedly uses darkness and light as spiritual imagery.
And honestly… both may be true.
Nicodemus came in darkness externally because darkness already existed internally.
He was spiritually conflicted.
Not hardened. Conflicted.
There is a difference.
A hardened heart attacks truth. A conflicted heart wrestles with it.
Nicodemus did not come mocking Jesus. He came searching.
Listen carefully to his opening words:
“Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that You do unless God is with him.” — John 3:2
The Greek says:
οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος
“We know You have come from God as a teacher.”
Did you catch that?
“We know.”
Not “I know.”
“We know.”
Meaning Nicodemus was not the only religious leader wrestling privately with the reality of Jesus.
There were others.
Silent believers. Hidden wrestlers. Men trapped between revelation and reputation.
And before condemning them too quickly, remember this:
Social death can terrify people almost as much as physical death.
Especially in religious systems.
Nicodemus had everything to lose.
Honor. Position. Influence. Relationships. Identity.
Following Jesus was not socially inspiring in that moment. It was dangerous.
We read Scripture knowing the resurrection happened. Nicodemus did not.
At that point, publicly aligning with Jesus could destroy his entire life.
And yet even while afraid… he kept moving closer.
That matters.
Some people only see cowardice in Nicodemus. Jesus saw movement.
Because God notices trembling steps too.
Then Jesus says something that completely dismantles religious pride.
“Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” — John 3:3
The Greek phrase is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
This can mean:
“born again” or “born from above.”
Jesus was confronting Nicodemus with a devastating truth:
Religious status cannot produce spiritual life.
Knowledge cannot regenerate the soul. Position cannot save. Tradition cannot resurrect the heart.
Nicodemus had mastered theology. But he had not yet surrendered.
And millions still live there today.
Biblically informed. Spiritually unmoved.
Church attendance without transformation. Bible knowledge without repentance. Christian language without crucifixion of self.
Jesus shattered all of it in one conversation.
And Nicodemus did not walk away.
That is important.
He stayed. He listened. He wrestled.
Because deep down, something inside him knew Jesus was speaking with authority no rabbi possessed.
The Hebrew concept of truth is deeply connected to the word:
אֱמֶת (emet)
Meaning: truth, faithfulness, stability, ultimate reality.
Jesus did not merely teach truth. He embodied emet.
And Nicodemus felt it.
That is why conviction became unavoidable.
Real encounters with Christ destabilize comfortable religion.
You cannot truly meet Jesus and remain emotionally untouched.
Eventually the pressure around Jesus intensified. Religious leaders became increasingly hostile. The atmosphere became politically volatile.
Then comes one of the most underrated moments in Scripture.
John 7.
The Pharisees wanted Jesus arrested. Officers returned empty-handed because even they were overwhelmed by Jesus’ words.
The leaders mocked them.
Then suddenly… Nicodemus speaks.
Not publicly as a disciple. Not fully surrendered yet. But he speaks.
John 7:51:
“Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?”
The Greek says:
μὴ ὁ νόμος ἡμῶν κρίνει τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ πρῶτον παρ’ αὐτοῦ
“Does our law judge the man unless it first hears from him?”
This was not a sermon.
It was a crack in fear.
A fracture in silence.
A respected Pharisee publicly interrupting an unjust condemnation.
Do you understand how dangerous that was?
Nicodemus was defending Jesus inside hostile territory.
He still was not openly declaring discipleship. But conviction was beginning to overpower self-preservation.
And this is where many people emotionally connect with Nicodemus.
Because courage often grows progressively.
Not everyone transforms overnight.
Peter denied Jesus publicly. Thomas doubted openly. Jonah ran. Elijah collapsed emotionally. Moses resisted calling.
Yet God kept pursuing them.
The modern world glamorizes instant transformation. Scripture often reveals gradual surrender.
Nicodemus defended Jesus before following Him publicly because conviction had already begun changing him internally.
The process was unfolding.
And maybe somebody reading this needed to hear that.
Because you think your fear disqualifies you.
But conviction itself may already be evidence God is drawing you.
You still hesitate. Still wrestle. Still struggle. Still fear people. Still battle compromise.
Yet you cannot walk away from Jesus completely.
Why?
Because truth keeps haunting you.
That is what happened to Nicodemus.
Jesus got inside his conscience.
And once Christ enters the conscience, pretending becomes exhausting.
Then comes the final appearance of Nicodemus.
And this moment changes everything.
Jesus is dead.
Crucified. Humiliated. Rejected.
Most disciples disappeared. Fear spread everywhere.
Following Jesus publicly now carried enormous danger.
Yet suddenly… Nicodemus appears again.
Not at night.
In daylight.
John 19:39 says:
“Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight.”
John intentionally reminds readers:
“who earlier had come by night.”
Why mention that?
Because the man hiding in darkness is no longer hiding.
The Greek says:
ἦλθεν δὲ καὶ Νικόδημος
“Nicodemus also came.”
He came.
When Jesus looked defeated. When association was costly. When reputation was threatened. When fear was justified.
He came.
And the amount of burial spices he brought was extravagant. Royal. Costly.
This was not secret admiration anymore.
This was public identification.
The fearful Pharisee had become courageous enough to honor a crucified Messiah.
And maybe that is the most beautiful part of the story.
Nicodemus did not arrive at boldness instantly.
He journeyed into it.
Slowly. Painfully. Honestly.
First curiosity. Then conviction. Then defense. Then devotion.
Some believers shame people still in process. Jesus did not.
Christ knew exactly how to bring Nicodemus from secrecy into surrender.
And perhaps some of the strongest believers today are still walking through that same painful transition.

There are people who quietly watch sermons after midnight. People secretly reading Scripture while pretending not to care. People hiding worship music under headphones. People terrified to tell family they believe. People trapped in intellectual pride while God keeps softening their heart. People defending Christianity publicly while privately battling whether to fully surrender.
Nicodemus speaks directly to them.
Because his story proves something powerful:
Jesus is patient with seekers who are honestly wrestling toward truth.
Not everyone begins bold. But many become bold after encountering Christ repeatedly.
The Hebrew word often connected to repentance is:
תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah)
Meaning: returning. Turning back. Coming home.
Nicodemus was slowly returning toward truth even before publicly identifying with Jesus.
And maybe right now you feel God pulling you the same way.
You cannot explain it.
But compromise feels heavier now. Sin feels emptier. Conviction hits harder. Worship affects you differently. The name of Jesus keeps disturbing your peace.
That is not accidental.
Christ still calls people out of darkness patiently.
The tragedy is not struggling.
The tragedy is resisting conviction until the heart becomes numb.
Nicodemus could have silenced his conscience forever. Instead, he kept moving closer to Jesus.
Even slowly.
And eventually hidden faith became visible devotion.
Somebody reading this has spent years intellectually near Jesus but emotionally distant from surrender.
You know verses. You understand theology. You can debate doctrine. But privately you still avoid complete obedience.
Nicodemus warns us that proximity to truth is not the same as transformation.
But he also gives hope.
Because people can change.
Fearful hearts can become courageous. Religious hearts can become reborn. Secret belief can become public devotion.
The Gospel still transforms people progressively.
And perhaps that is why Nicodemus defended Jesus before following Him publicly.
Because conviction was growing faster than his courage.
Until eventually courage caught up.
And maybe yours will too.
Be honest. This story probably felt closer to home than you expected.
Some people are not far from Jesus. They are just one surrendered step away from finally stepping into the light.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Ipinagtanggol ni Nicodemus si Jesus Bago Siya Sumunod Nang Hayagan
Maingay ang Jerusalem noong mga panahong iyon.
Hindi dahil sa pagsamba.
Kundi dahil sa takot.

May mga bulung-bulungan sa bawat sulok. May mga relihiyosong lider na pilit pinoprotektahan ang kanilang kapangyarihan. May mga taong namamangha sa mga himala ni Jesus. May iba namang gusto Siyang patahimikin.
At sa gitna ng lahat ng iyon… may isang lalaking unti-unting winawasak ng katotohanan.
Ang pangalan niya ay Nicodemus.
Hindi siya ordinaryong tao.
Isa siyang Pariseo. Isang guro ng Israel. Isang lalaking may reputasyon. May impluwensya. May pangalan.
At iyon mismo ang dahilan kung bakit mahirap sundan si Jesus.
Dahil kung susunod siya kay Cristo nang hayagan… maaaring mawala ang lahat.
Sa Juan 3:1, maingat siyang ipinakilala:
“May isang taong mula sa mga Fariseo, na ang pangalan ay Nicodemo, isang pinuno ng mga Judio.”
Sa orihinal na Griyego:
ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων (archōn tōn Ioudaiōn)
Ang salitang archōn ay nangangahulugang:
pinuno, may kapangyarihan, may impluwensya.
Hindi simpleng relihiyoso si Nicodemus. Bahagi siya ng sistemang kumokontrol sa relihiyon ng Israel.
Pero may isang bagay kay Jesus na hindi niya matakasan.
Hindi siya mapalagay.
Dahil may kakaibang awtoridad si Jesus.
May katotohanang hindi kayang pantayan ng relihiyon.
Kaya isang gabi… lihim siyang pumunta kay Jesus.
At maraming tao ang agad siyang hinuhusgahan dahil doon.
“Bakit sa gabi?” “Bakit hindi siya naging matapang agad?”
Pero kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao pa rin hanggang ngayon ang katulad niya.
Tahimik na naniniwala. Tahimik na naghahanap. Tahimik na lumalaban sa takot.

May mga taong nanonood ng preaching nang madaling araw pero walang nakakaalam. May mga taong gustong sumunod kay Jesus pero takot sa sasabihin ng pamilya. May mga gustong magbago pero natatakot mawala ang dating buhay.
Si Nicodemus ang larawan ng taong hinahabol na ng Diyos… pero hindi pa handang isuko ang lahat.
Sa Juan 3:2, sinabi:
οὗτος ἦλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτὸς
Ibig sabihin:
“Pumunta siya kay Jesus sa gabi.”
Oo, gabi iyon literal.
Pero sa Ebanghelyo ni Juan, madalas ding simbolo ang dilim.
Dilim ng takot. Dilim ng pagdududa. Dilim ng pusong hindi pa tuluyang sumusuko.
Hindi lumapit si Nicodemus kay Jesus para kutyain Siya. Lumapit siya dahil may bumabagabag na sa kanyang konsensya.
Pakinggan ang sinabi niya:
“Rabbi, nalalaman naming ikaw ay gurong mula sa Diyos…” — Juan 3:2
Sa Griyego:
οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος
“Alam naming galing Ka sa Diyos.”
Pansinin mo iyon.
Hindi niya sinabi:
“Ako.”
Kundi:
“Kami.”
Ibig sabihin… hindi lang si Nicodemus ang lihim na naniniwala.
May iba pang relihiyosong lider na nakakakita rin kung sino talaga si Jesus.
Pero takot sila.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… nakakatakot talaga minsan ang pagsunod kay Cristo.
Dahil may mga taong mawawala. May mga relasyong masisira. May reputasyong babagsak. May pride na kailangang mamatay.
Kaya bago natin husgahan si Nicodemus… tandaan natin:
Hindi lahat ng transformation ay biglaan.
May mga taong dahan-dahang dinadala ng Diyos palabas ng dilim.
At iyon mismo ang ginawa ni Jesus kay Nicodemus.
Sinabi ni Jesus:
“Malibang ang tao’y ipanganak na muli ay hindi niya makikita ang kaharian ng Diyos.” — Juan 3:3
Sa Griyego:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
Maaaring isalin bilang:
“ipanganak na muli” o “ipanganak mula sa itaas.”
Winawasak ni Jesus ang maling akala ni Nicodemus.
Na sapat na ang relihiyon. Na sapat na ang kaalaman. Na sapat na ang posisyon.
Hindi.
Kailangan ng bagong puso.
At milyon-milyong tao pa rin ngayon ang nasa parehong sitwasyon.
Maraming alam tungkol sa Diyos. Pero hindi pa sumusuko sa Diyos.
May Bible verse sa bio. Pero walang tunay na repentance. May church attendance. Pero walang pagbabago.
At habang kausap ni Jesus si Nicodemus… unti-unting winawasak ang kanyang pride.
Pero hindi siya umalis.
Nanatili siya.
Dahil kahit natatakot siya… alam niyang may katotohanang hindi niya kayang takasan.
Pagdating ng Juan 7, lalo pang lumala ang galit ng mga Pariseo kay Jesus. Gusto na nila Siyang ipahuli.
At doon nangyari ang isang napakahalagang eksena.
Biglang nagsalita si Nicodemus.
Hindi pa siya public disciple. Hindi pa siya handang ipahayag ang lahat.
Pero ipinagtanggol niya si Jesus.
Juan 7:51:
“Hinahatulan ba ng ating kautusan ang isang tao nang hindi muna siya dinirinig?”
Sa Griyego:
μὴ ὁ νόμος ἡμῶν κρίνει τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ πρῶτον παρ’ αὐτοῦ
Hindi ito simpleng legal argument.
Ito ay unang bitak sa kanyang takot.
Unang pagkakataong pinili niyang manindigan kahit kaunti.
At minsan… doon nagsisimula ang tapang.
Hindi agad sa entablado.
Kundi sa maliliit na desisyong hindi na kayang manahimik ng konsensya.
Maraming tao ang gustong instant transformation.
Pero madalas sa Biblia… proseso ang surrender.
Unti-unti. Masakit. Totoo.
At baka iyon mismo ang kailangan marinig ng isang tao ngayon.
Dahil akala mo disqualified ka dahil natatakot ka pa.
Pero baka ang conviction na nararamdaman mo ay ebidensya nang kinikilos ka ng Diyos.
Hindi mo na ma-enjoy ang dating kasalanan. Hindi ka na mapalagay. Hindi mo maalis si Jesus sa isip mo.
Bakit?
Dahil kapag pumasok na si Cristo sa konsensya ng tao… mahirap nang bumalik sa dating dilim.
Pagdating ng Juan 19, namatay na si Jesus.
Pinako. Tinanggihan. Pinahiya.
At karamihan sa mga alagad… nagtago.
Pero si Nicodemus?
Lumabas.
Hindi na sa gabi.
Kundi hayagan.
Juan 19:39:
“Dumating din si Nicodemo, na noong una’y pumunta kay Jesus sa gabi…”
Bakit pa binanggit ni Juan ang “gabi”?
Dahil gusto niyang ipakita:
Hindi na nagtatago ang dating takot.
Ang lalaking dating lihim kung maniwala… ngayon ay handa nang maiugnay kay Cristo kahit patay na Siya.
At napakalaki ng dala niyang pabango para sa paglilibing.
Mahal. Marangal. Parang para sa hari.
Hindi na ito simpleng curiosity.
Ito na ay devotion.
At baka iyon ang pinakamagandang bahagi ng kwento.
Hindi naging matapang si Nicodemus overnight.
Unti-unti siyang binago ni Jesus.
Mula curiosity. Patungong conviction. Patungong pagtatanggol. Patungong surrender.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito na nasa gitna rin ng prosesong iyon.
Hindi ka pa perfect. Hindi ka pa matapang lagi. Hindi mo pa ma-let go lahat.
Pero hindi mo na rin kayang lumayo kay Jesus.
Dahil may katotohanang patuloy kang hinahabol.
Ang Hebrew word para sa repentance ay:
תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah)
Ibig sabihin:
pagbabalik. Pag-uwi. Paglapit muli sa Diyos.
At iyon ang nangyayari kay Nicodemus.
Unti-unti siyang bumabalik sa liwanag.
At baka ikaw rin.
Maging totoo ka.
Mas malapit siguro sa puso mo ang kwentong ito kaysa inaamin mo.
May mga taong hindi malayo kay Jesus. Takot lang silang tuluyang lumabas sa dilim.
